hook_text: The sunlight on your skin left the Sun eight minutes ago. But the energy in it was made thousands of years before that.
clip_script: On a Durban beach the sand burns your feet. That heat left the Sun eight minutes and twenty seconds ago, crossing 150 million kilometres of empty space. But its story starts much earlier. The Sun is a star, a ball of hydrogen and helium plasma 109 times wider than Earth. It is not on fire; there is no oxygen to burn. In its core, at fifteen million degrees, the crushing weight of the Sun squeezes hydrogen nuclei so hard that they fuse into helium. Each new helium nucleus weighs slightly less than the four hydrogens that made it, and that missing mass becomes energy, four million tonnes of it every second. That energy then wanders outward through the dense interior for thousands of years before it escapes as light. So the warmth on your skin today began in the core of a star before the pyramids were built.
visual_style: A whiteboard beach with sun rays, then a cutaway of the Sun with a glowing core, hydrogen nuclei fusing into helium, a zigzag path out through the layers, and a straight ray to Earth.
pacing: Warm opening, a dramatic zoom into the core, then a long journey out.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and explain how the Sun shines.
